'NOBEL GLAS 3I ATLAS', SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-11: #1742 named, 'a scientific notebook and critical meta-analysis published on November 6, 2026, by Nobel Glas and Orin Trace via the Lagrange Observatory'; the ATA drift sign; the thirteen at 1665.53–1668.46 MHz against false-acceleration frames, short of a transmission; the nondetections composed as proof of natural origin; the Endogenous Sophon series. One link, the Observatory's page.
Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds for the findings. At the heteronym and the object, the Overview names the notebook by its title, its makers and its date, and composes from the Lagrange Observatory's page: the ATA paper's positive drift window against the negative drift a tone on the object would carry; the thirteen in the Green Bank cadence of December 2025 at 1665.53–1668.46 MHz, set against false-acceleration frames and stopped short of a transmission; the public statements and Overviews composing conditional nondetections as proof of natural origin; the series it extends, The Endogenous Sophon, as the page and the notebook name it. Four things move. (1) A quotation without a source: the teams concluding "nothing was found", where the page has 'each found nothing it judged worth following up'; the judgement drops out of the quoted verdict. (2) The investigation is given to one person, 'researcher Lee Sharks identified 13 data clusters', where the page has 'by Lee Sharks with two machine collaborators, Claude and ChatGPT' and the notebook gives the Green Bank work to Claude. (3) The thirteen keep their place 'near' the hydroxyl lines and lose 'and off them' (the nearest 54 kHz from the comet-frame OH), and lose the page's 'It does not replicate in sixteen held-out channels or at Parkes'; 'unaddressed anomalies' stands where the page gives an unreplicated excess. (4) The operator's reading, 'almost perfunctory', which the notebook keeps as his ruling apart from what the instruments say (§9.12, §12.9), is composed as the authors' argument, with 'to satisfy a consensus' added.

The publication reviews public radio astronomy data and critiques the methodology used by mainstream research teams to rule out artificial or technological signals from the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. Core Focus & Key Findings * Critique of Existing Search Filters: The notebook argues that three major teams published radio searches of 3I/ATLAS concluding "nothing was found," but their data filtering was overly narrow. For example, the Allen Telescope Array (ATA) paper filtered hits assuming a specific positive drift rate. Because a tone fixed directly to the moving interstellar object would actually drift negatively, the filter essentially removed the exact signal it was supposed to look for. * "The Thirteen" Anomaly: Running a target search using public Green Bank Telescope data from December 2025, researcher Lee Sharks identified 13 data clusters matching the comet's frame near the hydroxyl (OH) line frequencies (1665.53–1668.46 MHz). While the notebook explicitly stops short of calling these a technological "transmission," it highlights them as unaddressed anomalies that did not match the false-acceleration baseline control frames. * Media and AI Oversimplification: Nobel Glas examines how scientific nuances were lost in public-facing summaries. They point out that Google AI Overviews and press releases stripped away the specific frequency constraints, drift assumptions, and mathematical limits of the initial studies—incorrectly framing conditional "nondetections" as definitive, absolute proof of a purely natural origin. Philosophical Stance The text positions itself as part of a series titled The Endogenous Sophon, questioning the limitations of modern radio astronomy. The authors argue that mainstream searches often perform a "perfunctory" search designed to economically rule out artificial origins to satisfy a consensus, rather than executing the rigorous, exhaustive data parsing required to actually find an anomalous signal. Would you like to know more about the 3I/ATLAS interstellar object itself (such as its extreme age and unusual carbon-dioxide composition), or are you more interested in the specific radio astronomy technicalities critiqued in the Nobel Glas notebook?
